title: Ottawa flyer business apologizes for its part in spreading 'known romance scam'
summary: An eastern Ontario flyer business is apologizing for delivering door hangers it now says are part of a "known romance scam."

blocks.text: An eastern Ontario flyer business is apologizing for delivering door hangers it now says are part of a "known romance scam."
Door hangers delivered in Ottawa claimed to be from someone looking for a life partner
An eastern Ontario flyer business is apologizing for distributing what it says is a 'known romance scam.' (Thumbs Up Flyers/Facebook)
The hangers claim to be from someone looking for a life partner and hoping to meet a "kind, loving, and sincere woman between the ages of 40 and 87" to marry.
CBC News started getting emails from east Ottawa residents on Tuesday about the flyers, and found similar ads with the same contact information in some American newspapers.
"We did not know this when we accepted the job, and we would never knowingly put something like this on our neighbours' doors," said Thumbs Up Flyers in social media post Thursday.
The company said it has stopped distributing the hanger, is reporting the incident to authorities and is reviewing how it screens its contracts.

Thumbs Up Flyers told CBC they were unable to do an interview, but in an email the company's co-owner Joseph Juratovac said that the client behind the hangers contacted them through their website and provided a finished design. Juratovac said the company believes the client provided a false name.
Juratovac said the company delivered about 3,000 of the hangers in Orléans on Nov. 24 and 25 before it stopped distribution.
Thumbs Up Flyers said people should not email the addresses on the flyers and should check on anyone they know who may have received one, especially if they're elderly or living alone.
Ottawa police told CBC News it's aware of the flyers and reminded the public of general precautions people can take to avoid romance fraud.

items: Red flags for romance scams that Ontario police want you to know about

blocks.text: Don't send money, assets or sensitive information to someone you have never met in person, police say.

The federal government's online safety website advises Canadians to be wary of strangers who express overwhelming affection, make excuses to avoid meeting in person, or claim to need money or information to get out of an urgent predicament.

Jenna Legge is a reporter with CBC in Ottawa. Before that, she worked as a journalist on Prince Edward Island, with earlier stints in Winnipeg and Toronto. She holds a master's degree in international journalism from City University of London, and also studied journalism, law and political science at Carleton University.
